findings.finding: The new test_harness test is supposed to assert the grandchild 'dead after the timeout on every platform' via lock_owner._pid_alive. On POSIX, _pid_alive is os.kill(pid, 0). After killpg the orphaned grandchild is reparented to init or a subreaper and stays a zombie until that process reaps it. os.kill(pid, 0) succeeds on a zombie, so _pid_alive returns True. A one-shot assertion right after run_tool returns is therefore racy on POSIX, and fails permanently in a container whose PID 1 does not reap. The plan does not mention bounded polling. The repo already has a polling precedent (`_wait_until_gone` in the acli reaper tests).
scenarios: Linux CI: run_tool returns before init has reaped the killed grandchild, and the assertion flakes.
A Docker-based run where PID 1 is not an init: the zombie is never reaped, and the test fails every time.
findings.suggested_fix: Poll `lock_owner._pid_alive(pid)` every 0.05s for up to ~10s, and fail only if the pid is still alive at the deadline. In the finally block, best-effort kill any survivor so a failing run does not leak it.

findings.finding: The taskkill mechanism does not cover the case POSIX killpg does: a timed-out child that has already exited while an orphaned descendant still holds the pipe. `taskkill /T /PID <child>` walks the live process tree from the child's PID. Once the child has exited it is not in the tree, so taskkill fails. The fallback proc.kill() does nothing to an exited process, and the descendant survives. That is exactly the 'pipe-holding grandchild survives on Windows' defect the Root cause names. The plan claims parity ('kills the child and its descendants … as on POSIX') without stating this limitation.
scenarios: A wrapper or launcher child exits after spawning a long-running worker that inherited stdout. communicate() times out on the open pipe, taskkill finds no process tree under the dead PID, and the worker leaks while the caller waits out another drain

findings.finding: The plan says `taskkill /F /T /PID <pid>` "kills the child and its descendants", but `/T` finds descendants by walking parent-PID links from a live PID. If the direct child has already exited when taskkill runs (it exits on its own between the timeout firing and the reap, or the fallback `proc.kill()` killed it first), taskkill can't find any orphaned grandchild. It returns non-zero ('process not found'), the fallback `proc.kill()` can't reach the grandchild either, and `communicate(timeout=drain)` then waits the full drain on the grandchild's pipe before logging a survivor. The plan doesn't state this limit, and neither the new unit test (argv + fallback only) nor the `test_harness` grandchild test (child still alive at timeout) covers it.
findings.location: Approach (this change) — `_proc.reap_process_group` off POSIX bullet; src/rebar/_proc.py
scenarios: A grounding/ACLI child prints its result and exits just as the timeout fires, leaving a background grandchild holding stdout. taskkill returns 128, `proc.kill()` is a no-op, and the caller waits the full `drain` and leaks the grandchild.
Fallback path: taskkill itself times out or is missing and `proc.kill()` runs. The grandchild survives, as it does today.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach bullet and the `reap_process_group` docstring, add: "Windows has no process group: `taskkill /T` walks parent-PID links, so it reaches descendants only while the direct child is still alive. If the child has already exited, orphaned grandchildren are not killed, and the drain timeout logs them as survivors." If full parity with `killpg` is needed, track a follow-up to put the child in a Job Object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE (ctypes, stdlib-only) instead of relying on taskkill.

findings.finding: Routing both git_locking locks through lock_kernel changes the POSIX locking primitive as well as the Windows one, and the plan does not say whether lock_kernel's POSIX leg uses the same primitive git_locking uses today. The existing `_acquire_fetch_coord_flock` uses flock. On Linux, flock and fcntl/lockf locks do not exclude each other. If the primitives differ, an old-version process and a new-version process sharing a store or common dir would hold the 'same' lock concurrently during an upgrade, and any external probe expecting flock would misread state. 'POSIX path unchanged' is stated only for _proc.

evidence: "falling back to `proc.kill()` when taskkill is missing or fails; then `communicate(timeout=drain)` drains the pipes and logs a survivor"
findings.finding: The taskkill path does not say that its failure or fallback is logged, nor how a taskkill timeout is classified. Only a post-drain survivor is logged. A missing taskkill, a non-zero exit, or a TimeoutExpired from the bounded taskkill call would silently degrade to proc.kill(), which leaves grandchildren alive. That is the original bug, now invisible.
scenarios: taskkill is absent from PATH in a restricted Windows environment; every timeout leaves orphaned grandchildren and no log says the tree-kill was skipped.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the taskkill call to catch FileNotFoundError, OSError and subprocess.TimeoutExpired and to check for a non-zero returncode. In each case log a warning ('taskkill tree-kill failed for pid %d: %s; falling back to proc.kill()') before calling proc.kill(). Capture taskkill's stdout and stderr so they do not leak to the console.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that lock_kernel's POSIX leg uses the same primitive and granularity as git_locking's current fcntl call (flock vs lockf), or justify the change and note mixed-version/intra-process exclusion behaviour.
evidence: "git_locking: take and release both locks through lock_kernel.take_exclusive / release_exclusive"
"Same bounded wait, same 'advisory, proceed on exhaustion' contract" — no statement on preserving the POSIX lock primitive or exclusion granularity
Existing function name `_acquire_fetch_coord_flock` implies flock semantics today
findings.finding:
Routing `_store_git_op_lock` and the fetch-coordination lock through `lock_kernel.take_exclusive` may change POSIX lock semantics, but the plan does not say whether it does. The current module uses its own fcntl leg (e.g. `_acquire_fetch_coord_flock`, which suggests `fcntl.flock`). If lock_kernel's POSIX leg uses a different primitive (`fcntl.lockf`/record locks), three things break:
- flock and lockf do not exclude each other on Linux.
- Record locks are per-process, so two threads in one process could both 'acquire'.
- A concurrently running older rebar (still on flock) against the same git common dir would no longer be excluded.
The plan states 'POSIX path unchanged' only for `_proc`, not for git_locking.
scenarios: Linux: an old rebar holds the fetch-coord lock via flock while the new rebar acquires it via lockf. Both proceed, and concurrent fetches race on the shared common dir (the bug-9305 class reappears).
Same process, two threads taking the per-store git-op lock under record-lock semantics: both succeed and the serialization is lost.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the disposition (proceed-unlocked/advisory vs propagate as fatal) for non-contention errors from take_exclusive/release_exclusive in git_locking.
evidence: "a platform with neither leg (NoExclusiveLegError) still proceeds unlocked"
"advisory, proceed on exhaustion" — no disposition for non-contention OSError from the msvcrt leg or from release_exclusive
findings.finding: The plan alters the git_locking acquisition failure arm without a complete disposition. Two outcomes are stated: NoExclusiveLegError means 'proceed unlocked', and bounded-wait exhaustion means 'proceed'. Not stated is what surfaces when `take_exclusive` raises any other error on the new msvcrt leg. On Windows this includes a PermissionError/sharing violation opening the lock file, for example from AV or indexer handles. Such an error could propagate as fatal and abort the git op, or be treated as transient like contention and proceed unlocked; the plan does not say which. Release failures are likewise unaddressed.
scenarios: Windows: opening or locking the lock file fails with a sharing violation. It is unspecified whether the fetch aborts or proceeds unlocked.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State per arm (taskkill timeout/failure, proc.kill failure, drain timeout) that reap_process_group is best-effort/non-raising and the caller still sees the original timeout disposition.
evidence: "taskkill /F /T /PID <pid> (bounded by grace + drain) ... falling back to proc.kill() when taskkill is missing or fails; then communicate(timeout=drain) drains the pipes and logs a survivor, as on POSIX"
findings.finding:
The new off-POSIX reap chain is taskkill /F /T, then proc.kill(), then communicate(timeout=drain). The plan does not state what the caller of `reap_process_group` sees in three cases:
- taskkill itself times out (it is bounded by grace+drain).
- proc.kill() raises after taskkill failed.
- The drain still times out.
The plan says only that a survivor is 'logged ... as on POSIX'. It does not state whether reap is non-raising (best-effort) on every arm, or whether a fallback failure can mask the original timeout disposition the caller is handling.
scenarios: Windows: taskkill hangs past grace+drain, then proc.kill() raises. If either exception escapes the reap, it could replace the caller's original timeout outcome.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: 'Every off-POSIX reap arm is best-effort. taskkill TimeoutExpired/OSError/non-zero exit falls back to proc.kill(); a proc.kill() OSError and a drain TimeoutExpired are logged, never raised. The caller's timeout result is unchanged.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the `_proc` approach, either adopt a Job Object (KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, created at spawn, with taskkill /T as fallback) or record why taskkill /T alone is enough for rebar's callers despite missing orphaned grandchildren.
evidence: Plan: "`taskkill /F /T /PID <pid>` (bounded by `grace + drain`) kills the child and its descendants, falling back to `proc.kill()`"
The plan never mentions Job Objects or any other way to contain the tree when the child is spawned.

Retrieved: foedrum#92 calls this 'a known Windows limit' and says a Job Object (kill-on-close) is the real fix. watchhub-comms#612 and software-factory PR #76 both use a Job Object and keep taskkill /T as the fallback.
src/rebar/_proc.py's own docstring calls the target 'pipe-holding descendants'.
findings.finding: The Windows tree kill uses `taskkill /F /T /PID <pid>` without considering Windows Job Objects (JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE / TerminateJobObject). Job Objects are the established way to kill a whole process tree on Windows, and several current projects keep taskkill /T only as the fallback.
findings.location: Approach (this change) — `_proc.reap_process_group` off POSIX bullet; src/rebar/_proc.py
scenarios: A grounding or ACLI child starts a grandchild that inherits stdout or stderr, then exits. `communicate()` times out because the grandchild still holds the pipe. taskkill /T on the dead child's PID cannot see the grandchild, the fallback `proc.kill()` does nothing, and the grandchild leaks. This is the bug the plan says it fixes.
